At 100% the ice has a paper or noise texture, but the light is flat. There is no specular, no falloff and no thickness at the floe edges, and the crack lines look like uniform vector strokes with a jittered edge.
There are only 3 shots in 30 s, and the longest is 13 s. The year-to-year changes inside the first shot are dissolves or swaps, not built transitions.
gaps: Motion: the strong idea (ice extent shown as melting stencil numerals, then a bar chart made of ice, then Greenland as the area lost) is told with one slow linear wipe repeated. There is no physical behaviour (cracking with anticipation, floes drifting with weight, settling), no camera or parallax, and no real transition between the three sections. The ice should break apart into the bars, and the bars should melt down into the Greenland map.

Pace and arc: the per-second change stays flat for 0–17 s, then has two isolated spikes (17 s and 23 s) before a static outro. The 2012 record low should be the peak of a deliberate build, and the half-built chart and the long holds are dead air against a world-class median shot of about 2.5 s.

Sound: there is a sustained drone or pad with only three broadband hits (about 4.2 s, 13.2 s and 17.9 s) and one riser from about 24.5 to 26.5 s. The hits at 13 s and 18 s roughly line up with the cuts, but there is no ice-specific sound design (cracks, groans, water lapping), little dynamic contour, and the ending fades instead of landing on the Greenland reveal.
